youtube.baslik: Directional Microphones and Noise Reduction | Lesson 183 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
What can a hearing aid do to help a person understand speech in noise? In this lesson we cover how directional microphones work, polar patterns, fixed and adaptive directionality, digital noise reduction, and the real-world effect of these features.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Ricketts, Bentler and Mueller, Essentials of Modern Hearing Aids; Bentler, Wu, Kettel and Hurtig, Digital noise reduction: outcomes from laboratory and field studies, International Journal of Audiology (2008); Stelmachowicz et al., Effects of digital noise reduction on speech perception for children with hearing loss, Ear and Hearing (2010); Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how directional microphones in hearing aids work and how to read polar patterns.
Then we will discuss digital noise reduction and the real effect of these technologies on speech perception in noise.

maddeler.metin: Hearing loss requires a better SNR

cumleler: People with sensorineural loss need a better signal-to-noise ratio than normal-hearing listeners for the same understanding in noise.
This difference is called signal-to-noise ratio loss, or SNR loss, and is measured with speech-in-noise tests.
A hearing aid amplifies speech, but it also amplifies noise coming from the same direction and at the same frequencies.
So gain alone does not fix understanding in noise.
Real benefit requires improving the ratio of speech to noise reaching the ear.
The main ways to do this are directional microphones, remote microphone systems and arranging the listening setting.
Digital noise reduction, as we will see shortly, contributes mostly to listening comfort.
An omnidirectional microphone picks up sound from all directions with roughly equal sensitivity.
A directional system uses two microphones on the aid, about one centimeter apart.
Sound from the front reaches the front microphone first, and the rear microphone a very short time later.
For sound from behind, the order is reversed: it reaches the rear microphone first.
The processor delays the rear microphone's signal briefly and subtracts it from the front microphone's signal.
If the delay is chosen correctly, sound from behind is present in both signals at the same moment and cancels out.
Sound from the front is not canceled, so the talker in front stands out against the noise behind.
This arrangement requires the two microphones to be lined up from front to back on the aid.
So a directional microphone does not always fit into very small in-the-ear aids.
A microphone's sensitivity by direction is shown with a polar pattern.
Here we unroll the pattern onto a flat graph: the horizontal axis is the angle, with zero degrees straight ahead and 180 directly behind.
The omnidirectional pattern is flat; sound from every angle is picked up with the same sensitivity.
In the cardioid pattern, sensitivity falls toward the back and reaches its lowest point directly behind; this point is called the null.
In the hypercardioid pattern, the nulls are at about 110 and 250 degrees, so it suppresses sound from the rear sides most.
The directivity index is the ratio of sensitivity to sound from the front to sensitivity to sound from all directions, in decibels.

cumleler.yazi: In theory it is about 4.8 decibels for a cardioid and about 6 decibels for a hypercardioid.
cumleler.ses: In theory it is about four point eight decibels for a cardioid and about six decibels for a hypercardioid.

cumleler: When the aid is worn, the head and pinna change the pattern; real values are usually lower.
A directional system formed by subtracting two microphones loses sensitivity at low frequencies.
This drop grows by about 6 decibels each time the frequency is halved.
The aid usually compensates with extra gain, but this also raises the microphone's internal noise.
In a quiet setting, this noise may be heard as a hiss, and directionality brings no expected benefit there.
So omnidirectional mode is often preferred in quiet settings.
Directional systems are also more sensitive to wind noise, which is why aids include wind noise management.
Omnidirectional mode is the baseline, with directionality switched off.
In fixed directional mode, the pattern is preset; for example, it always works as a cardioid or hypercardioid.
In this mode, the best result comes when the noise source falls at the null of the pattern.
With adaptive directionality, the aid continually estimates the direction of the strongest noise in the rear half.
It then steers the null toward that direction; as the noise source moves, the pattern changes too.
Automatic systems classify the sound of the setting and switch to omnidirectional in quiet and directional in noisy speech settings.
Some aids can also wirelessly combine the microphones of both ears to form narrower directionality.
Which mode switches on when can be seen and adjusted in the aid's software.

maddeler.metin: Noise behind or to the sides
Lab benefit shrinks in real life

cumleler: The benefit of a directional microphone is greatest when the person faces the talker and the talker is relatively close.
Noise sources should be behind or to the sides; if noise comes from the same direction as the talker, directionality cannot help.
In a reverberant room, sounds reflect from every direction, so the effect of directionality decreases.
As the talker moves beyond the critical distance, more of the sound reaching the ear comes from reflections, and the benefit shrinks.
In the lab, directionality easily shows a benefit of a few decibels for understanding in noise.
In real life, however, the benefit users perceive is usually smaller.
Young children do not always face the talker and also learn language by overhearing, so directionality is used carefully with them.
Digital noise reduction, or DNR, estimates in each channel whether the signal resembles speech or noise.
The level of speech rises and falls several times per second with the rhythm of syllables, at around 4 hertz.
The level of steady noise, such as an air conditioner or engine hum, hardly fluctuates at all.
By looking at the depth and rate of this fluctuation, the aid estimates the signal-to-noise ratio in each channel.
Gain is reduced in channels where noise dominates; channels where speech dominates are protected.
In this example, gain has been lowered by a few decibels in the low-frequency channels, where the hum is strongest.
But speech and noise present in the same channel at the same time cannot be separated; if gain drops, both drop together.
So DNR cannot change the signal-to-noise ratio within a channel.
Research shows that DNR improves listening comfort and noise tolerance in noisy settings.

cumleler.yazi: In the 2008 study by Bentler and colleagues, users also found listening easier with DNR switched on.

cumleler: Some studies suggest that DNR may reduce listening effort.
On the other hand, no clear improvement in speech intelligibility in noise has usually been shown.
In other words, DNR does not make speech more intelligible; it makes the setting more tolerable.
Studies with children have not reported clear evidence that DNR harms speech perception.
This information is important for setting the user's expectations realistically.
The most effective way to understand speech in noise is a remote microphone system, which brings the microphone close to the talker's mouth.
A remote microphone largely removes the loss caused by distance and reverberation.
Directional microphones give an improvement of a few decibels under suitable conditions.
Moving closer to the talker and facing them improves both the signal-to-noise ratio and lipreading.
In a restaurant, sitting with your back to the noise source or choosing a quiet corner are also simple but effective strategies.
DNR does not replace these methods; it accompanies them for comfort.
In counseling, explaining these strategies together with the technology improves the user's real-world success.

sahneler.metin: Tell users that directionality only works when they face the talker. Use a speech-in-noise test to set expectations in advance.
cumleler: A tip from the field: directional microphones and noise reduction are the features users most often have wrong expectations about.
Tell the user clearly that directionality only works when they turn to face the talker.
A speech-in-noise test before fitting shows the person's SNR loss and what can realistically be expected.
For people with a large SNR loss, bring up remote microphone systems early.
At the follow-up appointment, check in the software which mode the aid switches to in which setting.

maddeler.metin: Directionality: two microphones and a delay
Benefit: talker in front, low reverberation

cumleler: In this lesson we saw that a directional microphone uses the time difference between two microphones to suppress sound from behind.
A polar pattern shows sensitivity by direction; the cardioid null is directly behind, and the hypercardioid nulls are at the rear sides.
The benefit of directionality is greatest when the talker is in front, the noise is behind and reverberation is low.
Digital noise reduction improves listening comfort but usually does not clearly change speech intelligibility in noise.

sahneler.soru: Where is the null of a cardioid pattern?
sahneler.aciklama: A cardioid pattern suppresses sound from directly _behind_ the most.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a cardioid polar pattern, in which direction is the null, the point of lowest sensitivity?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: directly behind, at 180 degrees.
In a hypercardioid pattern, the nulls are at about 110 and 250 degrees, that is, at the rear sides.
